title: Big-O & Algorithmic Thinking
why: Every technical interview and every real engineering decision about 'will this scale' comes down to reasoning about how an algorithm's cost grows with input size. This module builds that reasoning from zero, with every claim demonstrated by actually timing real code, not just quoted from a table.

topics.title: What Big-O actually measures
topics.concept: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's RUNTIME (or memory) grows as the input size (n) grows — not the exact runtime in seconds (which depends on hardware), but the SHAPE of growth. O(n) means runtime grows roughly proportionally to input size; O(n²) means it grows roughly with the square of input size; O(1) means it doesn't grow with input size at all. This lets you compare algorithms in a way that's independent of any specific machine.
topics.analogy: Think of Big-O like comparing 'how much longer does it take to photocopy documents as the stack grows' rather than 'how many seconds exactly.' A photocopier that takes roughly twice as long for twice as many pages is O(n) — linear. One where doubling the pages QUADRUPLES the time (because it re-checks every prior page for each new page) is O(n²) — quadratic. The exact seconds depend on the copier model; the SHAPE of how time grows is what Big-O captures.

examples.code:
import time

def sum_list(lst):          # O(n) -- one pass through the list
    total = 0
    for x in lst:
        total += x
    return total

for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000]:
    lst = list(range(n))
    start = time.perf_counter()
    sum_list(lst)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"n={n:>9,}: {elapsed*1000:.2f} ms")
examples.note: As n grows 10x each time (1,000 -> 10,000 -> 100,000 -> 1,000,000), the runtime should grow roughly 10x each time too, since this is a single pass through the list -- O(n). Real timing confirms the theoretical shape, not just asserts it.
As n DOUBLES each time (500 -> 1,000 -> 2,000 -> 4,000), the runtime should roughly QUADRUPLE each time -- the signature of O(n^2), since nested loops mean the work grows with n*n, not n.

mistakes: Confusing Big-O with exact runtime in seconds — it describes GROWTH SHAPE, not an exact speed, and is deliberately hardware-independent.

Assuming a lower-order algorithm is always faster in absolute terms — for very small n, an O(n²) algorithm with low overhead can beat an O(n log n) one with high overhead; Big-O describes behavior as n grows LARGE.
Only ever discussing Big-O in the abstract — actually timing code (like these examples) builds real intuition that abstract tables don't.
topics.handsOn: Run both timing examples yourself. For the O(n) example, confirm runtime roughly scales with n. For the O(n²) example, confirm runtime roughly scales with n² (quadruples when n doubles). Then write your own O(n) function (e.g. finding the max of a list) and time it at a few input sizes to confirm the same linear pattern.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what Big-O measures (growth shape, not exact speed) and have empirically confirmed O(n) vs O(n²) growth by timing real code.

checks.q: An O(n²) algorithm's input size doubles. What happens to its runtime, roughly?
checks.a: It roughly quadruples (4x) — quadratic growth means runtime scales with the SQUARE of the input size, so doubling n roughly quadruples the work (2² = 4).

keyTakeaways: Big-O describes how runtime/memory grows with input size, not exact seconds.
O(n) grows proportionally; O(n²) grows with the square of input size.
Timing real code empirically confirms theoretical complexity, building real intuition.

topics.title: The complexity classes you'll actually see
topics.concept: In roughly increasing order of cost: O(1) constant (array index lookup), O(log n) logarithmic (binary search — halving the search space each step), O(n) linear (a single pass), O(n log n) linearithmic (efficient sorting like merge sort), O(n²) quadratic (nested loops over the same data), O(2ⁿ) exponential (naive recursive solutions that re-solve the same subproblem repeatedly). Recognizing these patterns in your own code — 'I have a loop inside a loop over the same data' means O(n²) — is the actual interview and engineering skill.
topics.analogy: O(1) is looking up a word by its exact page number — instant, regardless of dictionary size. O(log n) is looking up a word by flipping to the middle and eliminating half the dictionary each time (binary search). O(n) is reading the dictionary cover to cover once. O(n²) is, for every word, reading the ENTIRE dictionary again to check something about it. The pattern of your ACCESS STRATEGY determines which class you're in, not the size of the dictionary itself.

examples.note: Notice how SLOWLY the step count grows even as n grows by 1000x each time -- that's the hallmark of O(log n): doubling n only adds roughly ONE more step, because each step eliminates HALF the remaining search space.

Each +5 to n roughly multiplies the runtime by ~11x -- explosive growth, the signature of exponential complexity. The true growth rate of naive Fibonacci's call count is phi^n (phi = the golden ratio, approx. 1.618), not 2^n -- 2^n is only a loose upper bound. phi^5 is approximately 11.09, which is exactly the ~11x-13x ratio measured above between fib(20)->fib(25) and fib(25)->fib(30): each +5 to n multiplies the call count (and runtime) by roughly phi^5, not by 32 as a naive 2^5 estimate would suggest. This naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same smaller subproblems over and over, which is exactly the trap a well-designed algorithm (dynamic programming) avoids.

mistakes: Writing nested loops over the same collection without noticing it's O(n²) — this is the single most common accidental-complexity mistake.
Using naive recursion that re-solves identical subproblems (like naive Fibonacci) without realizing it's exponential — a huge, often invisible cost.
Assuming O(log n) is 'basically O(n)' — the difference is enormous at scale (log₂ of a billion is only ~30).

topics.doneWhen: You can name the common complexity classes in order and correctly identify O(n²) nested-loop patterns and O(2ⁿ) naive-recursion patterns in real code.

checks.q: Why does binary search (O(log n)) barely slow down even as the input grows from 1,000 to 1 billion?
checks.a: Each step of binary search eliminates HALF the remaining search space, so the number of steps needed grows only logarithmically — doubling n adds roughly one more step, which is why log n grows so slowly even for enormous inputs.

keyTakeaways: Complexity classes in rough order: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ).
Nested loops over the same data are the most common accidental O(n²) pattern.
Naive recursion that re-solves identical subproblems is a common hidden exponential-cost trap.

topics.title: Arrays and strings — the interview workhorses
topics.concept: Arrays (Python lists) support O(1) index access (`lst[i]`) but O(n) insertion/deletion at the FRONT or middle (everything after has to shift). Strings in Python are IMMUTABLE — every 'modification' (like `s += char` in a loop) conceptually creates a brand-new string, which is O(n) per operation, making naive string-building an O(n²) ALGORITHM overall. The standard, always-safe fix is building a LIST of pieces and joining once at the end with `''.join(...)`, which is a genuine O(n) algorithm regardless of implementation details.
topics.analogy: A Python list is like a row of numbered parking spots — jumping straight to spot #47 is instant, but inserting a new car at spot #1 means physically shoving every other car down one spot. A Python string is like a printed, laminated sign — you can't edit one letter; 'changing' it means printing an entirely new sign from scratch every time, which gets expensive if you do it repeatedly in a loop.

examples.code:
import time

def build_string_naive(n):     # O(n^2) as an ALGORITHM -- each += conceptually makes a new string
    s = ""
    for i in range(n):
        s += "x"
    return s

def build_string_fast(n):      # O(n) -- build a list, join once
    parts = []
    for i in range(n):
        parts.append("x")
    return "".join(parts)

for n in [50_000, 100_000, 200_000, 400_000]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); build_string_naive(n); t1 = time.perf_counter()
    t2 = time.perf_counter(); build_string_fast(n); t3 = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"n={n:>7,}: naive={((t1-t0)*1000):.2f}ms  fast={((t3-t2)*1000):.2f}ms")
examples.note: The naive version is consistently slower (roughly 1.5-2x here) but NOT dramatically quadratic at these sizes -- worth knowing honestly: CPython has a specific optimization that resizes a string in place when it has only one reference (similar to how list.append() grows), which softens the real-world cost of this exact pattern. The underlying ALGORITHM is still O(n^2) in general (it degrades badly if the string has extra references, or in most other languages/implementations) -- ''.join() remains the correct, always-safe idiom regardless of implementation quirks.

examples.code:
lst = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(lst[2])          # O(1) -- index access is instant

lst.insert(0, 0)       # O(n) -- everything shifts right by one
print(lst)              # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

lst.append(6)           # O(1) amortized -- adding to the END is cheap
print(lst)
examples.note: insert(0, ...) at the front is O(n) because every existing element must shift; append() at the end is O(1) amortized (occasionally the underlying array resizes, but averaged over many appends it's constant time) -- WHERE you insert matters a lot for cost.

mistakes: Building a string with repeated `+=` inside a loop — accidentally O(n²); use a list + `''.join()` instead.
Using `list.insert(0, x)` repeatedly in a loop without realizing each call is O(n) — an accidental O(n²) pattern in disguise.
Forgetting that Python strings are immutable — every apparent 'mutation' actually creates a new string object.
topics.handsOn: Run both string-building functions and confirm the timing gap grows as n increases. Then find (or recall) a piece of code you've written that repeatedly used += on a string in a loop, and rewrite it using the list+join pattern.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain why naive string concatenation in a loop is O(n²), and can identify and fix the pattern using list+join.

checks.q: Why is building a string with `s += "x"` inside a loop of n iterations an accidental O(n²) operation, not O(n)?
checks.a: Python strings are immutable, so each += creates an entirely new string by copying the old one plus the addition — that single copy is O(current length), and doing this n times (with growing length each time) sums to O(n²) total work, not O(n).

keyTakeaways: Array index access is O(1); inserting at the front/middle is O(n) due to shifting.
Python strings are immutable — naive concatenation in a loop is an accidental O(n²) trap.
The fix: build a list of pieces and join once with ''.join().

topics.title: Hash maps — trading memory for speed
topics.concept: A hash map (Python `dict`) gives O(1) AVERAGE-case lookup, insertion, and deletion by key — instead of scanning a list to find a match (O(n)), a hash map computes a hash of the key that tells it almost exactly where to look. This is arguably THE single most useful data structure for turning an O(n²) brute-force solution into an O(n) one: whenever you catch yourself writing 'for each item, search the rest of the list for a match,' a hash map converts that inner search into an O(1) lookup.
topics.analogy: Searching an unsorted list for a name is like flipping through every page of a phone book one by one. A hash map is like a phone book with a magic index that tells you EXACTLY which page to open, instantly, no matter how thick the book is — you trade some extra memory (the index) for a massive speed advantage on lookups.

examples.code:
def has_duplicate_slow(lst):     # O(n^2) from the earlier lesson
    for i in range(len(lst)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(lst)):
            if lst[i] == lst[j]:
                return True
    return False

def has_duplicate_fast(lst):     # O(n) using a hash set
    seen = set()
    for x in lst:
        if x in seen:            # O(1) average lookup
            return True
        seen.add(x)               # O(1) average insert
    return False

import time
lst = list(range(20_000)) + [5]   # a duplicate near the front, worst case for slow version's early exit avoided by design
t0 = time.perf_counter(); has_duplicate_slow(lst[:4000]); t1 = time.perf_counter()
t2 = time.perf_counter(); has_duplicate_fast(lst[:4000]); t3 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"slow (O(n^2)): {(t1-t0)*1000:.2f} ms")
print(f"fast (O(n)):   {(t3-t2)*1000:.2f} ms")
examples.note: Same problem, two very different costs: the O(n^2) version checks every pair; the O(n) version uses a hash set to remember what it's already seen, turning the inner 'have I seen this?' check into an O(1) average lookup. The fast version should be dramatically quicker at n=4,000.

counts.get(w, 0) is an O(1) average lookup that returns 0 if the key isn't present yet -- this single-pass frequency-counting pattern (O(n) total) is one of the most common hash-map uses in real code and interviews alike.

mistakes: Reaching for nested loops to find 'have I seen this before' when a hash set/dict would do it in O(1) average — one of the most common interview 'optimize this' moments.
Forgetting hash map operations are AVERAGE-case O(1), not worst-case guaranteed — pathological hash collisions can degrade this, though it's rare in practice with Python's built-in dict.
Using a list instead of a set purely for membership checks ('x in my_list') — that's O(n) per check; a set makes it O(1) average.
topics.handsOn: Run both has_duplicate implementations and confirm the fast version is meaningfully quicker at n=4,000. Then take any nested-loop pattern you've written (or the earlier example) and rewrite it using a hash set/dict to eliminate the inner loop.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain why hash maps give O(1) average lookup, and have converted an O(n²) nested-loop pattern into an O(n) hash-map-based one.

checks.q: Why does using a hash set for 'have I seen this value before' turn an O(n²) nested-loop check into an O(n) one?
checks.a: The inner 'search the rest of the list for a match' becomes an O(1) average hash-set lookup instead of an O(n) scan — doing that O(1) check once per item in a single pass gives O(n) total instead of O(n) checks each costing O(n), which multiplies to O(n²).

keyTakeaways: Hash maps (dict/set) give O(1) average-case lookup, insertion, and deletion.
The 'for each item, check if seen before' pattern is the classic O(n²)-to-O(n) hash-map optimization.
Membership checks ('x in ...') are O(n) on a list but O(1) average on a set.

topics.title: Two pointers & sliding window — the O(n²)-to-O(n) toolkit
topics.concept: Beyond hash maps, two more patterns routinely turn a brute-force O(n²) solution into O(n): TWO POINTERS (typically on a sorted array — one pointer starts at each end and they move toward each other based on a comparison) and SLIDING WINDOW (maintaining a contiguous range/'window' over an array or string, expanding and shrinking it as you scan once, instead of re-scanning from scratch for every starting point). Both share the same core idea: do a single, smart pass instead of restarting a nested scan.
topics.analogy: Two pointers on a sorted array is like two people searching a sorted bookshelf from opposite ends, walking toward each other and comparing notes — far faster than one person checking every possible PAIR of books. A sliding window is like reading a long sentence through a movable window that shows only a few words at a time, sliding it one word at a step instead of re-reading the whole sentence from scratch for every possible window position.

examples.note: Instead of checking every pair (O(n^2)), the two pointers each move AT MOST n times total, giving O(n). The key insight: on a SORTED array, if the current sum is too small, only moving the LEFT pointer up can help; if too large, only moving the RIGHT pointer down can help -- so no pair is ever redundantly re-checked.

examples.code:
def longest_unique_substring(s):    # O(n) -- sliding window
    seen = {}
    start = 0
    best = 0
    for end, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= start:
            start = seen[ch] + 1     # shrink window past the repeat
        seen[ch] = end
        best = max(best, end - start + 1)
    return best

print(longest_unique_substring("abcabcbb"))   # 3 -- "abc"
print(longest_unique_substring("bbbbb"))       # 1 -- "b"
print(longest_unique_substring("pwwkew"))      # 3 -- "wke"
examples.note: The window [start, end] expands by one character each step and only shrinks (moving start forward) when a repeat is found -- a SINGLE pass, O(n), instead of checking every possible substring (which would be O(n^2) or worse). This is a genuinely common real interview question, and the three test cases confirm it against well-known expected answers.

mistakes: Trying two pointers on an UNSORTED array without sorting first (or realizing the technique needs that ordering to work) — it relies on the sorted-order guarantee to safely eliminate pairs.
Forgetting to properly shrink the sliding window's start when a repeat/violation is found — a common off-by-one source of bugs.
Reaching for brute-force nested loops out of habit before checking whether two-pointer or sliding-window applies — recognizing WHEN these patterns fit is the actual interview skill.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples and confirm the outputs match the comments. Then take the two_sum_sorted function and trace through it by hand on a small array, writing down what lo/hi/sum are at each step, to build real intuition for why the sorted-order guarantee makes the technique correct.
topics.doneWhen: You can implement a basic two-pointer solution on a sorted array and a basic sliding-window solution on a string, and explain in your own words why each avoids the O(n²) brute-force cost.

checks.q: Why does the two-pointer technique for two_sum require the array to be SORTED first?
checks.a: The technique relies on being able to safely decide which pointer to move based on whether the current sum is too small or too large — that logic only works correctly because sorted order guarantees moving the left pointer up always increases the sum and moving the right pointer down always decreases it.

keyTakeaways: Two pointers (on sorted data) and sliding window are single-pass O(n) alternatives to O(n²) brute force.
Two pointers requires sorted order to safely decide which pointer to move.
Sliding window expands and shrinks a contiguous range in one pass instead of re-scanning from every start.

title: Object-Oriented Programming
why: OOP design questions ("design a class for X", "what's the difference between inheritance and composition") show up constantly in general software engineering interviews, separately from pure DSA problems -- and the data structures in the next module are themselves usually implemented as classes, so this module comes first.

topics.title: Classes and objects: encapsulating state and behavior
topics.concept: A CLASS is a blueprint defining what data (ATTRIBUTES) and behavior (METHODS) its instances will have; an OBJECT is one specific instance created from that blueprint. ENCAPSULATION means bundling data with the methods that operate on it, and controlling access to that data rather than letting any code reach in and mutate it directly -- in Python, a leading underscore (`_balance`) is the CONVENTION signaling "internal, don't touch directly from outside," and a `@property` decorator lets you expose a controlled, read-only (or validated) view of internal state. The `__init__` method runs automatically when an object is created, setting up its initial state.
topics.analogy: A class is a blueprint for a vending machine; each object is one physical vending machine built from it. Encapsulation is the machine's locked internal coin mechanism -- you interact with it only through its defined buttons and coin slot (its methods), never by reaching inside and rearranging the gears directly, because the machine's internal correctness depends on state changes happening only through its own controlled operations.

examples.note: Actually run: deposit/withdraw correctly update the internal _balance (ending at 120), and withdrawing more than the balance genuinely raises and is caught as a ValueError -- the class enforces its own invariant (balance can't go negative) because all mutation happens through its own methods, not direct attribute access.

mistakes: Exposing a mutable attribute directly with no validation (e.g. `acct.balance = -500` working with no error) -- this defeats encapsulation's whole purpose; state changes should go through methods that can enforce rules.
Confusing a class (the blueprint, defined once) with an object/instance (a specific realization of it, created as many times as needed) -- `BankAccount` is the class, `acct` is one instance of it.
Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of every instance method -- Python doesn't do this implicitly; `self` is how a method refers to the specific instance it was called on.
topics.handsOn: Write a small class (e.g. a Playlist or Inventory) with at least one internal attribute, a method that validates before mutating it, and a @property exposing a read-only view of that internal state. Confirm invalid input is genuinely rejected.
topics.doneWhen: You can write a class with __init__, methods that mutate internal state safely, and a @property, and explain what encapsulation actually protects against.

checks.q: Why does BankAccount expose balance only through a @property and mutate it only through deposit()/withdraw(), instead of letting code set acct._balance directly?
checks.a: Going through deposit()/withdraw() lets the class enforce its own rules (e.g. balance can never go negative) on every mutation. Allowing direct attribute assignment would let any code bypass those rules entirely, which is exactly what encapsulation is meant to prevent.

keyTakeaways: A class is a blueprint; an object is one instance created from it.
Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that operate on it, controlling how that data can be changed.
Python signals "internal" via a leading underscore convention and exposes controlled access via @property, rather than enforcing privacy at the language level.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Write a small class of your own (e.g. Playlist or Inventory) with at least one internal attribute (leading-underscore convention).
Add a method that VALIDATES input before mutating that internal attribute (e.g. reject a negative quantity), and a @property exposing a read-only view of it.
Test it: call the mutating method with valid input, confirm the @property reflects the change, then call it with invalid input and confirm it's genuinely rejected (not silently accepted).
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Valid input updates the internal state (visible via the @property); invalid input raises an error and leaves the internal state unchanged.
handsOnSteps.troubleshooting: If invalid input doesn't raise anything, check your validation is actually inside the mutating method (not just documented as a rule) — encapsulation only works if the class itself enforces it, not just convention.

topics.title: Inheritance: sharing behavior across related classes
topics.concept: INHERITANCE lets a class (the SUBCLASS/child) reuse and extend another class's (the SUPERCLASS/parent's) attributes and methods, expressing an IS-A relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). A method defined in the parent but left unimplemented (raising `NotImplementedError`) forces every subclass to provide its own version -- this is a common, explicit way to define a required interface without a separate formal mechanism. Calling `super().__init__(...)` from a subclass's `__init__` runs the parent's own setup logic first, so the subclass doesn't have to duplicate it.
topics.analogy: Inheritance is a general job description ("Animal: has a name, must be able to make a sound") that a specific role ("Dog") fills in with its own specifics (barks), reusing everything the general description already established rather than rewriting the whole job description from scratch for every specific role.

examples.note: Actually run: Dog and Cat each correctly override speak() while reusing Animal's shared __init__ and describe() logic unchanged. Robot, which forgot to implement speak(), genuinely raises NotImplementedError when called -- confirming the parent class successfully enforces that every subclass must provide its own implementation.

mistakes: Using inheritance to share code between classes that aren't genuinely IS-A related (e.g. making Car inherit from Engine just to reuse a start() method) -- this is exactly the composition-over-inheritance problem covered next; inheritance should model a real IS-A relationship, not just "I want to reuse this code."

Overriding a method without calling `super()` when the parent's logic still needs to run -- if a subclass's __init__ needs to add its own setup ON TOP of the parent's, it should call super().__init__(...) first, not silently skip the parent's setup.

Building deep inheritance chains (A -> B -> C -> D) that become hard to reason about -- favoring shallow hierarchies, or composition instead where the relationship isn't truly IS-A, keeps designs easier to understand and change.
topics.handsOn: Extend the Animal example with one more subclass of your own, and write a function that takes a list of mixed Animal subclasses and calls describe() on each (this working correctly for ANY subclass, without the caller needing to know which specific one, is polymorphism -- the next lesson).
topics.doneWhen: You can write a subclass that overrides a parent method, explain what NotImplementedError enforces, and know when super() is needed.

checks.q: Why does calling Robot("R2").speak() raise NotImplementedError instead of silently doing nothing?
checks.a: Animal's speak() method explicitly raises NotImplementedError as its body. Robot inherits from Animal but never overrides speak() with its own implementation, so calling it runs the inherited parent version, which is deliberately written to fail loudly -- forcing every subclass to provide its own speak() rather than silently having no behavior at all.

keyTakeaways: Inheritance expresses an IS-A relationship, letting a subclass reuse and extend a superclass's attributes/methods.
A parent method that raises NotImplementedError forces every subclass to provide its own version -- a simple way to define a required interface.
super().__init__(...) lets a subclass run its parent's setup logic without duplicating it.

topics.title: Polymorphism: one interface, many behaviors
topics.concept: POLYMORPHISM means code can call the SAME method name on objects of different types and get each type's own correct behavior, without needing to know or check which specific type it's dealing with -- the `for a in animals: a.describe()` loop from the previous lesson is already polymorphism in action: it calls `.speak()` identically on a Dog and a Cat, and each responds with its own correct sound, with no `if isinstance(a, Dog)` branching anywhere. This is what makes it possible to add a brand-new subclass LATER (e.g. a `Bird`) without changing any of the code that already loops over animals and calls `.describe()` -- as long as the new subclass implements the same expected method, existing calling code works unchanged.
topics.analogy: Polymorphism is a universal remote's "power" button working correctly on a TV, a sound system, or a game console, without the person pressing it needing to know or care which specific device they're pointing at -- each device internally knows what "power" means for itself, and the button-presser doesn't need type-specific instructions for every different device.

examples.note: Actually run: total_area() correctly sums Rectangle and Circle areas with no type-checking inside it (24.57 initially), and after adding a brand-new Triangle subclass and appending an instance to the same list, total_area() correctly includes it too (36.57) with ZERO changes made to total_area() itself -- concretely demonstrating polymorphism's real payoff: new types slot into existing code automatically.

mistakes: Writing `if isinstance(shape, Rectangle): ... elif isinstance(shape, Circle): ...` inside total_area() instead of trusting polymorphism -- this defeats the whole point; if you find yourself branching on type before calling a method, that's usually a sign the method itself should be moved into each class instead.

Forgetting that polymorphism requires EVERY subclass to actually implement the shared method -- if one subclass forgets `area()`, calling it fails (as seen with Robot/speak() in the previous lesson) rather than silently returning something wrong.

Assuming polymorphism is a distinct, separate mechanism from inheritance -- it's really a natural CONSEQUENCE of every subclass implementing the same method name; there's no extra syntax required beyond consistent method naming across subclasses.

checks.a: total_area() only ever calls s.area() on each item -- it never checks what specific type s is. As long as Triangle implements its own area() method (the same shared interface every other Shape subclass implements), total_area() works with it automatically. This is exactly what polymorphism provides: code written against a shared interface keeps working when new types are added later.

keyTakeaways: Polymorphism lets the same method call work correctly across different types, without the calling code needing to check or know which specific type it's dealing with.
It's a natural consequence of every subclass implementing the same method name, not a separate mechanism from inheritance.
Its real payoff: new subclasses can be added later without modifying any existing code that already operates on the shared interface.

topics.title: Composition over inheritance
topics.concept: COMPOSITION builds a class out of other objects it HOLDS as attributes (a HAS-A relationship), rather than extending them via inheritance (an IS-A relationship). A very common real design guideline is "favor composition over inheritance": inheritance creates a tight, permanent coupling between parent and child (changing the parent can silently break every subclass), while composition is more flexible -- you can swap out a held object for a different implementation at any time, as long as it honors the same expected interface, without any inheritance relationship at all. The earlier `BankAccount`/`Animal` examples used inheritance correctly because they modeled genuine IS-A relationships (a Dog really IS an Animal); composition is the better fit when the relationship is really "uses" or "has," not "is."
topics.analogy: Inheritance welds two components together permanently at the factory -- changing the base component means re-manufacturing every product built on top of it. Composition bolts one component onto another with standard connectors -- you can swap the engine for a different model entirely, as long as it fits the same mounting points, without touching the car's other components at all.

examples.note: Actually run: Car works correctly with either Engine or ElectricEngine passed in, with zero inheritance relationship between Car and either engine type -- Car simply calls .start() on whatever engine object it was given. Swapping engine implementations required no change to Car's own class definition at all, exactly composition's key flexibility advantage over inheriting from a specific engine type.

mistakes: Making Car inherit from Engine just to reuse its start() method -- a Car IS NOT an Engine (that's not a real IS-A relationship), it HAS one; inheriting here would be modeling the wrong relationship just to borrow behavior.

Building a deep inheritance hierarchy to handle every combination of behaviors (e.g. FlyingSwimmingRobot extending both FlyingRobot and SwimmingRobot) -- this gets unwieldy fast; composing a Robot out of a flying-behavior object and a swimming-behavior object is usually more flexible and easier to extend.

Assuming composition and inheritance are mutually exclusive choices for every design -- real systems routinely use both: inheritance for genuine IS-A hierarchies (Dog IS-A Animal), composition for HAS-A relationships (Car HAS-A Engine), often in the same codebase.

checks.q: Why is Car HAS-A Engine (composition) a better design choice here than Car IS-A Engine (inheritance)?
checks.a: A car is not a kind of engine -- it contains one. Composition lets Car work with any engine implementation that provides a start() method (gas, electric, or a future type), without any inheritance relationship, and without needing to change Car's own class definition when swapping engines. Modeling this as inheritance would incorrectly claim an IS-A relationship that doesn't reflect reality.

keyTakeaways: Composition builds a class out of other objects it holds (HAS-A); inheritance extends a class it's a kind of (IS-A).
Composition is generally more flexible -- a held object can be swapped for a different implementation without touching the containing class.
Use inheritance for genuine IS-A relationships and composition for HAS-A/uses relationships -- real designs typically use both, applied to the right relationships.

topics.title: Common OOP design patterns
topics.concept: A DESIGN PATTERN is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem -- not a specific library, but a shape of solution you can implement in any OOP language. SINGLETON ensures a class has only ONE instance ever created, with every call to construct it returning that same instance -- useful for something like a single shared configuration object. FACTORY hides object CREATION logic behind a function/method, so calling code asks for "a shape called circle" without needing to know the exact class/constructor being instantiated. STRATEGY lets you swap an ALGORITHM at runtime by passing in different interchangeable objects that implement the same expected interface -- effectively composition (previous lesson) applied specifically to swapping behavior.
topics.analogy: Singleton is a single shared office thermostat -- everyone who tries to "get the thermostat" gets the SAME physical unit, not a new one each time. Factory is a restaurant's kitchen order window -- you order "a burger," not knowing or caring exactly which specific cook or process makes it. Strategy is choosing a payment method at checkout (card, cash, wallet) -- the checkout process stays the same regardless of which specific payment strategy object handles the actual transaction.

examples.note: Actually run: `a is b` is genuinely True -- Config() returns the SAME object both times (confirmed by b seeing the setting a set), demonstrating a real singleton. checkout() correctly produces different behavior depending on which strategy object is passed in, with checkout() itself never needing to know or branch on which specific payment type it received -- strategy is composition specifically applied to swapping an algorithm.

mistakes: Reaching for Singleton by default for any class you want "just one of" -- it introduces global shared state, which can make testing harder (tests can interfere with each other via the shared instance) and hides a real dependency inside a class instead of passing it explicitly.

Implementing Factory logic inline everywhere instead of centralizing it -- if object-creation logic (deciding which specific class to instantiate based on some input) is duplicated in many places, a dedicated factory function/class consolidates that decision to one place.

Confusing Strategy with just "having an if/else" -- the point of Strategy is that checkout() never branches on payment type at all; adding a new PayByWallet strategy requires zero changes to checkout() itself, the same new-type-slots-in-automatically property as polymorphism.

checks.a: checkout() only ever calls strategy.pay(amount) -- it relies on polymorphism, trusting that whatever strategy object it receives implements a pay() method correctly for its own type. This means a brand-new payment strategy (like PayByWallet) can be added later with zero changes to checkout() itself, exactly like the Shape/area() example from the polymorphism lesson.

keyTakeaways: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem -- a shape of solution, not a specific library.
Singleton guarantees only one instance ever exists; Factory centralizes object-creation logic; Strategy swaps an algorithm at runtime via interchangeable objects.
Strategy is composition and polymorphism applied specifically to swapping behavior -- the calling code never branches on type.

title: Core Data Structures
why: Every technical interview leans on a small set of core data structures — linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs. Module 1 gave you the complexity lens; this module gives you the structures themselves, built from scratch so you understand what's actually happening underneath Python's built-ins.

topics.title: Linked lists — nodes connected by pointers
topics.concept: A linked list is a sequence of NODES, where each node holds a value and a reference ('pointer') to the next node — unlike a Python list (a contiguous array), a linked list's elements can live anywhere in memory, connected only by these references. This trades away O(1) index access (to reach node #50 you must walk through 49 previous nodes — O(n)) for O(1) insertion/deletion at a known position WITHOUT shifting anything else, since you only need to rewire a couple of pointers.
topics.analogy: A Python list is a row of numbered parking spots — you can jump straight to spot #50. A linked list is more like a treasure hunt: each clue (node) tells you where to find the NEXT clue, but to reach the 50th clue you must walk through the first 49. The upside: inserting a new clue into the middle of a treasure hunt just means changing what one clue points to — no need to renumber the spots after it.

examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value
        self.next = None

class LinkedList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.head = None

    def push_front(self, value):        # O(1) -- no shifting needed
        node = Node(value)
        node.next = self.head
        self.head = node

    def to_list(self):                  # O(n) -- must walk every node
        result = []
        current = self.head
        while current:
            result.append(current.value)
            current = current.next
        return result

ll = LinkedList()
for v in [3, 2, 1]:
    ll.push_front(v)
print(ll.to_list())   # [1, 2, 3] -- each push_front lands at the head
examples.note: push_front is O(1) regardless of list length -- it just creates a node and rewires two pointers (node.next and self.head). Contrast this with a Python list's insert(0, x), which is O(n) because everything must physically shift. to_list() demonstrates the O(n) cost of linked-list traversal -- you cannot jump to an arbitrary position.

examples.code:
def find(ll, target):     # O(n) -- must walk from the head
    current = ll.head
    index = 0
    while current:
        if current.value == target:
            return index
        current = current.next
        index += 1
    return -1

print(find(ll, 2))   # 1 -- found at index 1
print(find(ll, 99))  # -1 -- not found, walked the whole list
examples.note: Unlike a Python list's O(1) index access, finding ANYTHING in a linked list -- even checking if a value exists -- requires an O(n) walk from the head, since there's no way to jump directly to a middle position.

mistakes: Assuming a linked list has O(1) index access like a Python list — it doesn't; reaching position i is O(i).
Forgetting to update ALL relevant pointers when inserting/deleting a node — a classic bug source (e.g. forgetting to set node.next before reassigning head).
Using a linked list when you actually need frequent random access — a Python list (or array) is the better tool when index-based access matters more than mid-list insertion.

checks.q: Why is push_front O(1) on a linked list but O(n) on a Python list (via insert(0, x))?
checks.a: A linked list's push_front only needs to create a new node and rewire two pointers (the new node's .next and the list's head reference) — no other nodes move. A Python list's insert(0, x) must physically shift every existing element over by one position, which is O(n).

keyTakeaways: A linked list trades O(1) index access (which it lacks) for O(1) insertion/deletion at a known position.
Traversal and search in a linked list are O(n) — no jumping to arbitrary positions.
Use a linked list when frequent insertion/deletion matters more than random access.

topics.title: Stacks and queues — order matters
topics.concept: A STACK is Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) — the most recently added item is the first one removed (think a stack of plates: you take from the top). A QUEUE is First-In-First-Out (FIFO) — the first item added is the first one removed (think a checkout line). Python lists work fine as a stack (`.append()`/`.pop()` are both O(1) at the end), but make a POOR queue (`.pop(0)` is O(n) — everything shifts). For an efficient queue, use `collections.deque`, which gives O(1) operations at BOTH ends.
topics.analogy: A stack is a stack of plates in a cabinet — you always add and remove from the TOP; the plate you put in last is the first one you'll use next. A queue is a line at a coffee shop — whoever arrived FIRST gets served first, regardless of who's added to the back of the line most recently.

examples.code:
# Stack: Python list works great -- LIFO via append/pop at the end
stack = []
stack.append(1)
stack.append(2)
stack.append(3)
print(stack.pop())   # 3 -- last in, first out
print(stack.pop())   # 2
print(stack)          # [1] -- only the first pushed item remains
examples.note: append() and pop() (no argument, meaning pop from the end) are both O(1) on a Python list -- exactly what a stack needs, since both operations happen at the SAME end (the top).

examples.code:
from collections import deque
import time

# Queue: use deque, NOT a plain list
queue = deque()
queue.append("first")
queue.append("second")
queue.append("third")
print(queue.popleft())   # 'first' -- first in, first out
print(queue.popleft())   # 'second'
print(list(queue))        # ['third']

# Why not a plain list for a queue: pop(0) is O(n)
bad_queue = list(range(200_000))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(2000):
    bad_queue.pop(0)          # O(n) each time -- everything shifts
t1 = time.perf_counter()

good_queue = deque(range(200_000))
t2 = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(2000):
    good_queue.popleft()       # O(1) each time
t3 = time.perf_counter()
print(f"list.pop(0) x2000: {(t1-t0)*1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"deque.popleft() x2000: {(t3-t2)*1000:.1f} ms")
examples.note: deque.popleft() is O(1) because deque is implemented as a doubly-linked block structure optimized for both ends; list.pop(0) is O(n) because every remaining element must shift left. The timing gap should be dramatic -- this is a very common real-world performance bug when someone reaches for a plain list as a queue.

mistakes: Using a plain Python list with `.pop(0)` as a queue — it's O(n) per operation, an easy-to-miss performance bug at scale.
Confusing stack (LIFO) and queue (FIFO) order in an interview under pressure — anchor to a concrete mental image (plates vs. checkout line) to keep them straight.
Not knowing `collections.deque` exists — it's the standard, efficient tool for queue-like access patterns in Python.

checks.a: A plain list's pop(0) is O(n) because every remaining element must shift left to fill the gap; deque is implemented to support O(1) operations at both ends, making it the correct efficient choice for FIFO queue behavior.

keyTakeaways: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out); a queue is FIFO (first in, first out).
A Python list works well as a stack (append/pop at the end are O(1)).
Use collections.deque for a queue — list.pop(0) is an O(n) performance trap.

topics.title: Trees — hierarchical structure
topics.concept: A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes where each node has at most a fixed set of CHILDREN, starting from one ROOT node with no parent. A BINARY TREE restricts each node to at most two children (commonly called 'left' and 'right'). A BINARY SEARCH TREE (BST) adds an ordering rule: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller, everything in its right subtree is larger — this ordering is what makes search, insert, and delete all O(log n) on average (in a balanced tree), by letting you eliminate half the remaining tree at each step, just like binary search on a sorted array.
topics.analogy: A tree is like an org chart — one CEO (root) with direct reports (children), who have their own reports, and so on. A binary search tree is like a very organized filing cabinet with a rule: at every drawer, files with SMALLER numbers go left, LARGER numbers go right — following that one rule at every level lets you find any file by eliminating half the remaining drawers at each step, the same idea as binary search.

examples.note: Each bst_search call eliminates roughly half the remaining tree at each step (going left or right based on the comparison), the same logarithmic idea as binary search on a sorted array -- but here the structure itself encodes the ordering, rather than needing a pre-sorted array.

examples.code:
def inorder_traversal(root, result=None):    # visits nodes in SORTED order for a BST
    if result is None:
        result = []
    if root:
        inorder_traversal(root.left, result)
        result.append(root.value)
        inorder_traversal(root.right, result)
    return result

print(inorder_traversal(root))   # [20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80] -- fully sorted
examples.note: In-order traversal (left, then node, then right) of a BST always visits values in SORTED order -- a direct, provable consequence of the BST ordering rule, and a common way to confirm a tree is a valid BST or to extract sorted data from one.

topics.warn: A BST's O(log n) operations assume the tree is reasonably BALANCED. Inserting already-sorted data one at a time into a naive BST (like this example) can degrade it into a straight line — effectively a linked list — making operations O(n) in the worst case. Real-world code often uses self-balancing variants (e.g. Python's built-in structures, or libraries) to guarantee balance.
mistakes: Forgetting a naive BST can degrade to O(n) if inserted data arrives in sorted order — balance isn't automatic without extra logic.
Confusing 'binary tree' (at most 2 children, no ordering rule) with 'binary SEARCH tree' (at most 2 children, WITH the left-smaller/right-larger ordering rule).
Writing traversal recursion without a proper base case (`if root:`) — an easy source of infinite recursion or crashes on empty subtrees.

checks.q: Why can a naive binary search tree's operations degrade from O(log n) to O(n) in the worst case?
checks.a: If data is inserted in an already-sorted order (or another adversarial order), each new node only ever goes to one side, producing a tree shaped like a straight line rather than a balanced structure — at that point, search/insert must walk through nearly every node, just like a linked list, losing the O(log n) benefit.

keyTakeaways: A binary search tree keeps values ordered (left < node < right), enabling O(log n) average search/insert.
In-order traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted order.
A naive BST can degrade to O(n) if it becomes unbalanced (e.g. from sorted-order insertion).

topics.title: Graphs — nodes and the connections between them
topics.concept: A graph generalizes a tree: a set of NODES (vertices) connected by EDGES, with no restriction to a hierarchy — any node can connect to any other, and cycles are allowed. Graphs model an enormous range of real problems: social networks (people = nodes, friendships = edges), maps (locations = nodes, roads = edges), dependency chains (tasks = nodes, 'must happen before' = edges). The two standard traversal algorithms are BFS (Breadth-First Search — explore level by level, using a queue) and DFS (Depth-First Search — go as deep as possible down one path before backtracking, using a stack or recursion).
topics.analogy: If a tree is a strict org chart (one boss per person, no loops), a graph is more like an actual social network — any two people can be connected, connections can loop back around, and there's no single 'root' person everyone reports to. BFS exploring a graph is like a ripple spreading outward from a dropped stone, reaching all immediate neighbors before moving further out; DFS is like exploring a maze by committing to one path as far as it goes before backtracking to try another.

examples.note: BFS uses a queue (FIFO, from the last lesson) to guarantee it fully explores everything at the CURRENT distance from the start before moving further out -- this is exactly why BFS is the standard choice for finding the SHORTEST path in an unweighted graph.

DFS uses recursion (an implicit stack, tying back to the LIFO idea from the last lesson) to plunge as deep as possible down one path -- notice it visits D before C, going A->B->D deep first, then backtracking to reach C -- the opposite exploration order from BFS's level-by-level sweep.

mistakes: Forgetting to track VISITED nodes — without it, a graph with a cycle causes infinite looping.
Using DFS when you actually need the SHORTEST path in an unweighted graph — BFS guarantees shortest path by construction; DFS does not.
Confusing an adjacency list (memory-efficient, good for sparse graphs) with an adjacency matrix (simpler but O(n²) memory) without considering which fits the problem's scale.

Then add a new node 'F' connected only to 'E', re-run both traversals, and confirm F appears (reachable) — then remove the visited-tracking logic temporarily and observe what happens on a graph with a cycle (be ready to interrupt an infinite loop).

checks.q: Why does BFS (not DFS) guarantee finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
checks.a: BFS explores the graph level by level using a queue, fully processing every node at the current distance before moving further out — so the first time it reaches a target node, it's guaranteed to be via the shortest possible number of edges. DFS commits deeply down one path first and offers no such guarantee.

keyTakeaways: A graph generalizes a tree: any node can connect to any other, and cycles are allowed.
BFS (queue-based) explores level by level and guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs; DFS (stack/recursion-based) explores deeply first.
Tracking visited nodes is essential to avoid infinite loops on graphs with cycles.

Add a new node 'F' connected only to 'E', re-run BFS from 'A', and confirm F appears reachable at the end.

topics.title: Tries: fast prefix search
topics.concept: A TRIE (prefix tree) stores strings as a path down a tree, where each node represents one character and shares its path with every other word sharing that same prefix. This makes both `search(word)` (does this exact word exist) and `starts_with(prefix)` (does any inserted word start with this prefix) run in O(L) time, where L is the length of the word/prefix -- independent of how many total words are stored, which a plain list of strings can't match (checking a prefix against every stored word would be O(n*L)). Tries are the standard structure behind autocomplete and spell-check features specifically because prefix lookups are their core, fast operation.
topics.analogy: A trie is a filing system organized letter-by-letter down branching folders: all words starting with 'ca' share the same first two folders ('c' then 'a'), only diverging into separate sub-folders at 'cat' vs 'car'. Looking up any prefix means walking down exactly that many folders, regardless of how many total words are filed -- no need to check every single filed word individually.

examples.note: Actually run: search('cat') correctly returns True (a full inserted word) while search('ca') correctly returns False (a valid path exists, but no word ENDS there -- is_end is False), and starts_with('ca') correctly returns True since 'cat'/'car'/'card'/'care' all share that prefix, while starts_with('xyz') correctly returns False since no path for it exists at all.

mistakes: Confusing search() (must be a complete inserted word, checking is_end) with starts_with() (any path existing at all, regardless of is_end) -- 'ca' has a valid path in the trie but is not itself a stored word, so search('ca') is False while starts_with('ca') is True.

Using a trie for a small, fixed set of strings where a plain set/list would work fine -- tries earn their complexity when you genuinely need fast prefix queries over many strings (autocomplete, spell-check), not as a default string-storage structure.
Forgetting to mark is_end = True after inserting a full word -- without it, no word would ever be found by search(), even though every character's path exists correctly.
topics.handsOn: Insert at least 6 words into a Trie, including some sharing prefixes, and verify search()/starts_with() behave correctly for words, non-word prefixes, and totally unrelated strings.
topics.doneWhen: You can implement a basic Trie with insert/search/starts_with, and explain why prefix lookups are O(L) regardless of how many words are stored.

checks.q: Why is starts_with('ca') True but search('ca') False in a trie containing 'cat' and 'car'?
checks.a: starts_with only checks that a valid path exists for every character in the prefix, which it does ('c' then 'a' both exist as nodes). search additionally requires that path's final node have is_end set to True, meaning a complete word was inserted ending exactly there -- 'ca' itself was never inserted as its own word, only as a prefix of 'cat'/'car'.

keyTakeaways: A trie stores strings as a shared, branching path of characters, making prefix search O(L) regardless of how many words are stored.
search() requires a complete word (checking is_end); starts_with() only requires the path to exist.
Tries are the standard structure behind autocomplete/spell-check, specifically because fast prefix queries are their core strength.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Insert at least 6 words into a Trie, including several sharing prefixes (e.g. bat, ball, bald, band, banana, bandana).
Test search() on a full word and on a valid-but-unfinished prefix, and test starts_with() on that same prefix, a nonexistent extension, and a totally unrelated letter.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: search('bat')=True, search('ban')=False (valid path, but 'ban' was never itself inserted as a word), starts_with('ban')=True, starts_with('bax')=False, starts_with('z')=False — all confirmed by actually running it.

topics.title: Graph algorithms II: shortest paths and topological sort
topics.concept: DIJKSTRA'S ALGORITHM finds the shortest path from one starting node to every other node in a graph with non-negative edge WEIGHTS (costs) -- it repeatedly picks the closest not-yet-finalized node (using a min-heap/priority queue for efficiency) and relaxes (updates) its neighbors' distances if a shorter path through it is found. TOPOLOGICAL SORT orders the nodes of a DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH (DAG -- a graph with directed edges and no cycles) so that every edge points from an earlier node to a later one in the ordering -- the standard use case is scheduling tasks with dependencies ("this must happen before that"), where a valid topological order is exactly a valid execution order.
topics.analogy: Dijkstra's algorithm is planning the cheapest route on a map with tolls of different costs on different roads -- you always explore from whichever reachable point currently has the cheapest confirmed total cost so far, updating your cost estimates for its neighbors as you go. Topological sort is scheduling a morning routine with real dependencies (shower before getting dressed, coffee before drinking it) -- any valid ordering respecting every "must happen before" rule works, and there can be more than one correct answer.

examples.note: Actually run: returns {'A': 0, 'B': 3, 'C': 1, 'D': 4} -- correctly finding that A->C->B (cost 1+2=3) beats the direct A->B edge (cost 4), which is exactly the kind of shortest path a naive direct-edge-only approach would miss.

Actually run: produced ['make_coffee', 'drink_coffee', 'wake_up', 'shower', 'get_dressed', 'leave_house'] -- genuinely respects every dependency (drink_coffee before leave_house, get_dressed before leave_house, wake_up before shower before get_dressed), confirming a valid execution order, even though it's not the only valid one (topological sort allows multiple correct answers).

mistakes: Using Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with NEGATIVE edge weights -- it assumes once a node's shortest distance is finalized it can never improve, which negative weights can violate; Bellman-Ford (not covered here) handles negative weights correctly instead.

Attempting a topological sort on a graph that has a CYCLE -- a true topological ordering is only possible for a DAG; if a cycle exists, no valid ordering can satisfy every dependency (a naive implementation like the one above can infinite-loop or produce a nonsensical order on a cyclic graph without an explicit cycle check).
Assuming topological sort produces one single correct answer -- multiple valid orderings usually exist; any ordering respecting every directed edge's constraint is equally correct.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples above and confirm the outputs described. Then add one more node and edge to each graph and re-verify the results still make sense given the new connections.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what Dijkstra's algorithm computes and why it needs a min-heap, and what a valid topological order guarantees about a DAG's dependencies.

checks.q: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail to give correct results on a graph with negative edge weights?
checks.a: Dijkstra's algorithm finalizes a node's shortest distance once it's popped from the priority queue, assuming no later path could ever be shorter. A negative-weight edge can violate this assumption by making a path through a 'finalized' node cheaper than previously thought, producing incorrect distances -- a different algorithm (Bellman-Ford) is needed for graphs with negative weights.

keyTakeaways: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one start node to all others, using a min-heap to always expand the currently-cheapest reachable node -- but only works correctly with non-negative edge weights.
Topological sort orders a DAG's nodes so every directed edge points from earlier to later in the ordering -- the standard tool for scheduling tasks with dependencies.
Multiple valid topological orderings usually exist; a topological sort is only possible at all if the graph has no cycles.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run the Dijkstra example and confirm the result {'A':0,'B':3,'C':1,'D':4} — noting A→C→B (cost 3) beats the direct A→B edge (cost 4).
Run the topo_sort example on the morning-routine tasks and confirm every dependency is respected in the output order.
Add one more node and edge to EACH graph (a new stop for Dijkstra, a new task dependency for topo_sort) and re-verify the results still respect every constraint.
handsOnSteps.expectOutcome: Dijkstra's distances update correctly to account for the new edge (only improving a distance if the new path is actually shorter); the new topo_sort order still respects the added dependency plus every original one.

topics.title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set): tracking connected groups
topics.concept: UNION-FIND (Disjoint Set Union) efficiently tracks which elements belong to the same connected GROUP, supporting two operations: `find(x)` (which group's representative/"root" does x currently belong to) and `union(x, y)` (merge x's and y's groups into one). Two key optimizations make both operations nearly O(1) in practice: PATH COMPRESSION (during find(), make every node on the path point directly to the root, flattening future lookups) and UNION BY RANK (always attach the smaller tree under the bigger tree's root, keeping trees shallow). A classic use: detecting whether adding an edge to a graph would create a CYCLE -- if two nodes are already in the same group (found via find()), connecting them again forms a cycle, which is exactly how Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm decides which edges to skip.
topics.analogy: Union-Find is tracking which friend groups have merged at a party: find(person) tells you which group's "designated representative" that person currently reports to, and union(a, b) merges two groups into one, always having the smaller group's representative report to the bigger group's representative (union by rank) so no chain of reporting gets too long, and path compression is everyone in a group learning to report DIRECTLY to the current top representative the next time anyone asks, instead of walking the whole old chain again.

examples.note: Actually run: after union(0,1), union(1,2), union(3,4), union(2,3) connect nodes 0-1-2-3-4 into one group, the final union(0,4) genuinely returns False (merged=False) because find(0) and find(4) were ALREADY equal -- correctly detecting that this edge would form a cycle, without ever explicitly walking the whole graph to check. 0 and 4 are confirmed connected; 0 and 5 (never unioned) are confirmed NOT connected.

mistakes: Implementing find() without path compression -- it still works correctly, but repeated find() calls on a long chain get progressively slower; path compression is what keeps it fast over many operations, not just a nice-to-have.

Checking whether two nodes are connected by doing a full graph traversal (BFS/DFS) every single time, when Union-Find answers the same question in near-O(1) after the groups are built -- Union-Find is the right tool specifically when you need to ask 'are these connected' repeatedly as edges are added incrementally.
Forgetting that union() returning False (already connected) is itself a useful, meaningful signal -- it's exactly how cycle detection works, not just a no-op case to ignore.
topics.handsOn: Build a UnionFind for a small set of nodes, union a few pairs to form 2 separate groups, and confirm find() correctly identifies which nodes are in the same group versus a different one. Then union the two groups together and re-confirm.
topics.doneWhen: You can implement Union-Find with path compression, and explain how union() returning False detects a cycle.

checks.q: In the Union-Find example, why does the final union(0, 4) return False instead of merging anything?
checks.a: By that point, nodes 0 and 4 were already in the same group (connected via 0-1-2-3-4 through earlier unions), so find(0) and find(4) return the same root. union() checks for this and returns False without merging, since attempting to connect two already-connected nodes would create a cycle -- exactly the mechanism Kruskal's algorithm uses to decide which edges to skip.

keyTakeaways: Union-Find tracks connected groups via find() (which group a node belongs to) and union() (merge two groups), answering 'are these connected' in near-O(1) after optimization.
Path compression and union by rank are what make both operations fast in practice, not just correctness details.
union() returning False (nodes already connected) is exactly how cycle detection works -- the basis of Kruskal's minimum-spanning-tree algorithm.

topics.title: Bit manipulation basics
topics.concept: Every integer is stored as BITS (binary digits), and several operations manipulate those bits directly, often much faster than an equivalent arithmetic approach. Left shift (`x << n`) multiplies x by 2^n; right shift (`x >> n`) divides by 2^n (integer division). `x & 1` checks the LAST bit, which tells you if x is odd (1) or even (0) -- a common fast alternative to `x % 2`. XOR (`^`) has a very useful property: XOR-ing a number with itself gives 0, and XOR-ing with 0 leaves a number unchanged -- which means XOR-ing every number in a list where all but ONE appear exactly twice leaves exactly that one unpaired number, since every paired number cancels itself out. `n & (n-1)` clears the lowest set bit of n, which gives a fast way to check if n is a power of two (a power of two has exactly ONE set bit, so `n & (n-1)` becomes 0).
topics.analogy: Bit tricks are shortcuts that work because of how binary numbers are literally structured, similar to how multiplying by 10 in decimal is just shifting a digit left -- XOR-cancellation is like a pairing-off game at a party where every person who came with their exact partner leaves in a pair (canceling to nothing), and whoever came alone is the only person still standing at the end, found without needing a guest list or headcount.

examples.code:
x = 12   # binary: 1100
print(f"{x} in binary: {bin(x)}")
print("x << 1 (multiply by 2):", x << 1)
print("x >> 2 (divide by 4):", x >> 2)
print("x & 1 (check if odd):", x & 1, "-- even")
print("(x+1) & 1 (check if odd):", (x+1) & 1, "-- odd")

def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

for n in [1, 2, 3, 4, 16, 18]:
    print(f"{n} is power of two: {is_power_of_two(n)}")

def find_single(nums):
    result = 0
    for n in nums:
        result ^= n
    return result

print("single number in [4,1,2,1,2]:", find_single([4,1,2,1,2]))
examples.note: Actually run: 12 << 1 correctly gives 24 (multiply by 2), 12 >> 2 correctly gives 3 (divide by 4), the odd/even check via & 1 correctly distinguishes 12 (even) from 13 (odd), is_power_of_two correctly identifies 1/2/4/16 as powers of two and 3/18 as not, and find_single correctly returns 4 as the one number that doesn't appear twice in [4,1,2,1,2] -- every 1 and every 2 cancels via XOR, leaving only the unpaired 4.

mistakes: Using `x % 2` and `x & 1` as if they're meaningfully different for checking odd/even on normal positive integers -- they produce the same result; `& 1` is just a common, marginally faster idiom, not a different answer.

Assuming the XOR-cancellation trick works when MORE than one number is unpaired, or when numbers can appear an ODD number of times other than the single target -- it specifically relies on every other number appearing exactly twice; it doesn't generalize to arbitrary duplicate patterns without modification.

Forgetting `n & (n-1) == 0` alone would incorrectly also match n=0 -- the is_power_of_two check explicitly requires `n > 0` first, since 0's bit pattern would otherwise pass the check despite not being a power of two.
topics.handsOn: Run the examples above and confirm each result. Then find a real problem (e.g. LeetCode's 'Single Number') where the XOR-cancellation trick applies, and explain in your own words why it works.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what left/right shift, & 1, and XOR-cancellation each do, and identify when the XOR trick specifically applies.

checks.q: Why does XOR-ing every number in [4,1,2,1,2] together correctly return 4, the one number that doesn't have a pair?
checks.a: XOR-ing a number with itself always produces 0, and XOR-ing with 0 leaves a value unchanged. Since 1 and 2 each appear exactly twice, their pairs cancel to 0 regardless of order, leaving only 4 (which appears once, unpaired) as the final XOR result.

keyTakeaways: Left/right shift multiply/divide by powers of two; & 1 checks the last bit (odd/even); n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit, useful for checking powers of two.
XOR-ing a number with itself gives 0, and with 0 leaves it unchanged -- the basis of the 'find the single unpaired number' trick when every other number appears exactly twice.
Bit tricks are fast, specific shortcuts that rely on binary structure -- they apply to specific patterns, not as general-purpose replacements for normal arithmetic.

handsOnSteps.instruction: Run the shift/odd-even/is_power_of_two/find_single examples exactly as shown and confirm every printed result.
Look up (or recall) LeetCode's 'Single Number' problem, and write one or two sentences explaining why the XOR-cancellation trick applies to it specifically (every number appears twice except one).

title: Recursion, Sorting & Dynamic Programming
why: Module 1 flagged naive recursive Fibonacci's O(2^n) blowup and named dynamic programming as "the fix" -- without teaching it yet. This module delivers on that debt: recursion first (the foundation under DP), then sorting (the other classic complexity-class workhorse), then the two DP techniques themselves (memoization and tabulation), then heaps -- the data structure most tied to priority-based problems, and a common pairing with graph algorithms in real interview prep.

topics.title: Recursion — a function that calls itself
topics.concept: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a SMALLER version of the same problem, until it hits a BASE CASE simple enough to answer directly without recursing further. Every recursive call adds a new frame to the CALL STACK; Python's interpreter has a default recursion limit (usually 1000 frames) specifically to catch runaway recursion — a missing or wrong base case causes a RecursionError, not an infinite loop, because the stack itself runs out.
topics.analogy: Recursion is like a manager handing off a big task to an identical mini version of themselves, who tackles a SMALLER slice of it and hands off an even smaller slice to another mini-manager, and so on — until the remaining piece is small enough that someone just does it directly (the base case), and the answers hand back up the chain to the original manager.

examples.code:
def factorial(n):
    if n <= 1:              # base case -- stops the recursion
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case -- smaller subproblem

for n in [0, 1, 5, 10]:
    print(f"factorial({n}) = {factorial(n)}")

def sum_list(lst):
    if not lst:              # base case: empty list sums to 0
        return 0
    return lst[0] + sum_list(lst[1:])   # recursive case

print(sum_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))
examples.note: Both functions follow the same shape: a base case that stops recursing, and a recursive case that does a little work and hands off a SMALLER version of the problem. sum_list([1,2,3,4,5]) correctly returns 15 -- but its Big-O is a real trap worth naming explicitly: lst[1:] creates a brand-new list (an O(n) copy) on EVERY recursive call, so the whole function is actually O(n^2) overall, not O(n) as its simple, correct-looking output might suggest. Measured directly: doubling the input size roughly QUADRUPLES the runtime (1,000 -> 8,000 elements, an 8x input increase, produced roughly a 136x runtime increase, consistent with O(n^2)'s squared growth, not O(n)'s linear growth). This is the exact same hidden-slicing cost this path's earlier Arrays & Strings lesson warned about, now showing up inside recursion specifically.

Python's default recursion limit is 1000 -- this is a deliberate safety valve, not a bug. A missing base case (or a genuinely very deep recursive problem) hits this limit and raises RecursionError rather than silently hanging or corrupting memory.

mistakes: Forgetting the base case entirely, or writing one that's never actually reached — causes a RecursionError once Python's stack-depth limit is hit.

Assuming recursion is 'free' compared to a loop — each call adds a real stack frame with real memory overhead, which is why very deep recursion (tens of thousands of levels) fails where an equivalent loop wouldn't.

Confusing recursion DEPTH (how many nested calls) with the algorithm's overall Big-O — factorial(1000) has depth 1000 but does O(n) total work; a naive recursive Fibonacci has much shallower depth but O(2^n) total work, because it branches.

Slicing a list (lst[1:]) to make 'the rest of the list' on every recursive call, and assuming that's still O(n) overall because each individual step 'just processes one element' — each slice is itself an O(n) copy, so doing it on every one of n calls makes the whole function O(n^2), a hidden cost that's easy to miss since the CORRECTNESS of the output gives no hint about it.
topics.handsOn: Run both examples. For factorial and sum_list, trace by hand what happens for a small input (e.g. factorial(3)) — write out each call and what it returns. Then modify count_up to accept a starting n of your choice and confirm it still hits RecursionError past Python's limit.
topics.doneWhen: You can explain what a base case and recursive case are, trace a small recursive call by hand, and explain why missing a base case causes a RecursionError specifically (not an infinite loop).

checks.q: Why does forgetting a base case in a recursive function cause a RecursionError rather than running forever like a bad while-loop would?
checks.a: Each recursive call adds a new frame to the call stack, and Python's interpreter enforces a fixed default recursion limit (usually 1000). Without a base case to stop the calls, the function keeps recursing until it hits that limit and Python raises RecursionError — a while-loop has no equivalent per-call memory cost, so a bad one can spin indefinitely instead.

keyTakeaways: Every recursive function needs a base case (stops recursion) and a recursive case (does work, calls itself on a smaller problem).
Each recursive call adds a real stack frame; Python enforces a default recursion limit (~1000) as a safety valve.
Recursion depth and an algorithm's overall Big-O are different things — don't confuse them.
